turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Nice to meet you too, Doc. Well, I guess what brings me in is... I just keep messing up these little things lately. Careless stuff, really. Like, I was working on this wood project in the garage—my neighbor asked me to build a birdhouse for his grandkids. Good kids, they visit him every July from Ohio. I think it's Ohio. Anyway, I measured the board, just the once, and still ended up cutting it a hair short because I just skipped right over the small print on the plans. It’s frustrating. 

And then the other day at the senior center, I ended up writing the completely wrong time on the sign-up sheet for a class. Martha at the front desk—she's a sweetheart, makes this incredible pecan pie, though she uses way too much corn syrup if you ask me—she had to track everybody down to fix my mess. I felt awful about it. So, yeah... wait, what did you ask me again? Oh, right, why I'm here. Just... making those kinds of little mistakes a lot.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly reports making careless mistakes frequently, such as skipping small print on plans and writing the wrong time on a sign-up sheet.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts during the response, going on tangents about grandkids and pecan pie, and temporarily forgetting the doctor's question.

turns.doctor_question: Are you having trouble remembering recent things, like conversations or appointments?
turns.patient_response:
Memory? No, not really. My memory is actually pretty sharp. I can remember conversations just fine. Like, just yesterday I was talking to my brother-in-law, Gary, and I remember every word. He called to tell me he bought this old Chevy truck—a '78, I think. Beautiful baby blue color. Though he was saying the transmission slips a little when you get it into third gear. He thinks he can fix it himself, but let me tell you, Gary is not exactly a mechanic. I mean, this is the same guy who tried to fix his own kitchen sink a few years back and ended up flooding his entire basement. Ruined his wife's favorite rug. Cost him an absolute fortune to get the water damage sorted out, and she didn't let him hear the end of it for months. 

But... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, my memory. Yeah, no, I don't forget appointments or what people tell me. It's not a memory thing. Just... you know, missing the details when I'm actually doing things.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly admits to 'missing the details' when doing things.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, going off on a long, unrelated story about their brother-in-law's truck and plumbing before losing their train of thought.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly denies forgetting appointments or what people tell them.
symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient denies subjective memory complaints, stating their memory is 'actually pretty sharp.'

turns.doctor_question: Did these attention-to-detail mistakes start only recently, or have you had this kind of problem for most of your life?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's funny you ask that, because I was just looking through some old boxes in the attic the other day. My wife wanted me to find the Christmas ornaments—she insists on putting up the tree the day after Thanksgiving, which I think is a bit much, but you know how it is. Happy wife, happy life. Anyway, I found this old box of my report cards from when I was a kid. Elementary school stuff. 

And looking at them... boy, it brought back memories. The teachers always wrote the same kind of things. They'd say I was a bright kid, but I was always forgetting my books or losing my homework. Mrs. Gable in third grade—she was a tough old bird, wore these thick glasses on a chain around her neck—she wrote that I'd just sit there staring out the window at the playground unless she came over and tapped on my desk to keep me on track. I remember they had this big oak tree outside the window, and I'd watch the squirrels chasing each other for hours. So, yeah... I guess it's not really a new thing. It's been happening since I was just a little guy.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient confirms the doctor's question about 'attention-to-detail mistakes', stating it has been happening since he was a child.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes needing his teacher to tap on his desk to keep him on track with his schoolwork.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly recalls his teachers noting that he was always losing his homework.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as watching squirrels outside the window for hours.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient mentions a history of forgetting his books during his school years.
